misconceptions.statement: After several heads in a row, tails is more likely on the next toss.
misconceptions.why: Students expect short runs to 'balance out' like the 50-50 ratio.
misconceptions.fix: Each toss is independent; the coin has no memory, so tails stays equally likely at 1/2.

probe.question: A fair coin shows heads 5 times in a row. What is the probability of tails on the 6th toss?

misconceptions.root_belief: nature corrects itself to even things out
misconceptions.source_hint: research on gambler's fallacy and representativeness heuristic (Kahneman-Tversky; Fischbein)

misconceptions.statement: After a streak of heads, heads is more likely next because the coin is 'hot'.
misconceptions.why: Students see a pattern in recent results and expect it to continue.
misconceptions.fix: Past tosses do not change a fair coin's chance; heads is still 1/2.

probe.question: A coin gave heads 4 times. What is the chance of heads next?

misconceptions.root_belief: recent patterns must continue
misconceptions.source_hint: research on hot-hand and recency beliefs in probability learning

misconceptions.statement: If a coin is tossed 10 times, it must give exactly 5 heads.
misconceptions.why: Students treat theoretical probability as a guaranteed result.
misconceptions.fix: Probability tells long-run tendency; in a few trials the number of heads can differ from half.

probe.question: A fair coin is tossed 10 times. How many heads will you get?

misconceptions.root_belief: a prediction is a guarantee
misconceptions.source_hint: research on outcome approach (Konold) in students' probability thinking

misconceptions.statement: If probability of rain is 0.7, it will definitely rain.
misconceptions.why: Students read high probability as certainty, wanting a yes/no answer.
misconceptions.fix: A probability of 0.7 means rain is likely but not sure; it is certain only at probability 1.

probe.question: P(rain tomorrow)=0.7. Will it rain?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will rain for sure

misconceptions.root_belief: a likely thing is a certain thing
misconceptions.source_hint: Konold's outcome approach: probability used to predict single outcomes

misconceptions.statement: Experimental probability = successes divided by the number of failures.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse ratio of success to failure with the fraction of all trials.
misconceptions.fix: Divide the number of times the event happened by the total number of trials.

probe.question: A die is rolled 20 times, a six appears 4 times. Find the experimental probability of a six.

misconceptions.root_belief: ratio compares parts, not part to whole
misconceptions.source_hint: research on part-part vs part-whole ratio confusion and odds in probability

misconceptions.statement: Total number of trials is the number of times the event did not happen plus one.
misconceptions.why: Students use the wrong denominator by ignoring some trials.
misconceptions.fix: The denominator is all trials, successes plus failures together.

probe.question: In 30 trials, a bulb was defective 3 times. Probability of defective?

misconceptions.root_belief: only counted items belong in the total

misconceptions.statement: Experimental probability from 10 trials is as reliable as from 1000 trials.
misconceptions.why: Students do not see that sample size affects stability of the ratio.
misconceptions.fix: With more trials the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical value, so large samples are better.

probe.question: Which gives a better estimate of P(head): 10 tosses or 1000 tosses?

misconceptions.root_belief: sample size does not matter
misconceptions.source_hint: research on law of large numbers and sample size insensitivity

misconceptions.statement: The experimental probability must exactly equal the theoretical probability.
misconceptions.why: Students think both methods are two ways to get one identical answer.
misconceptions.fix: Experimental values vary and only tend to approach the theoretical value with many trials.

probe.question: A die rolled 60 times shows 8 sixes. Is something wrong because 8 is not 10?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the die must be unfair

misconceptions.root_belief: estimates must equal exact values

misconceptions.statement: Sample space of a die has only the outcomes we are interested in.
misconceptions.why: Students list only the favourable outcomes as the sample space.
misconceptions.fix: The sample space lists every possible outcome, favourable or not.

probe.question: Write the sample space for rolling a die and getting an even number.

misconceptions.root_belief: only what matters to question exists

misconceptions.statement: Tossing two coins has 3 outcomes: 2 heads, 2 tails, 1 head and 1 tail.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore order and treat HT and TH as the same.
misconceptions.fix: There are 4 outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT; coins are distinct so HT and TH differ.

probe.question: Two coins are tossed. What is P(one head and one tail)?

misconceptions.root_belief: order does not matter
misconceptions.source_hint: research on compound-event sample space errors (Fischbein; Batanero)

misconceptions.statement: Rolling two dice, the sum 7 is as likely as sum 12, since each is one outcome.
misconceptions.why: Students list sums as outcomes rather than ordered pairs.
misconceptions.fix: Sum 7 happens in 6 pairs, sum 12 in only 1 pair out of 36, so 7 is far more likely.

probe.question: Two dice are thrown. Compare P(sum 7) and P(sum 12).

misconceptions.root_belief: every listed result is equally likely
misconceptions.source_hint: research on the equiprobability bias (Lecoutre) with sums of two dice

misconceptions.statement: Any experiment with two outcomes has probability 1/2 for each.
misconceptions.why: Students assume outcomes always share chance equally.
misconceptions.fix: Equal probability holds only if outcomes are equally likely; otherwise use actual counts.

probe.question: A bag has 1 red and 9 blue balls. What is P(red)?

misconceptions.root_belief: two options means fifty-fifty
misconceptions.source_hint: equiprobability bias documented by Lecoutre in probability research

misconceptions.statement: A bag with 3 red and 7 blue balls gives equal chance to red and blue colours.
misconceptions.why: Students count colours, not balls, as outcomes.
misconceptions.fix: Each ball is equally likely, so red has 3/10 and blue 7/10.

probe.question: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue balls. P(red)?

misconceptions.root_belief: categories count equally regardless of size
misconceptions.source_hint: research on equiprobability bias and sample-space construction

misconceptions.statement: On a spinner with unequal sectors, each sector is equally likely.
misconceptions.why: Students count sectors and ignore their sizes.
misconceptions.fix: Outcomes are equally likely only when sectors are equal; larger sectors have greater probability.

probe.question: Spinner has 2 sectors, one 3/4 of circle. P(small sector)?

misconceptions.root_belief: count of items matters, not their size

misconceptions.statement: Probability of an event is favourable outcomes divided by unfavourable outcomes.
misconceptions.why: Students mix odds with probability.
misconceptions.fix: Divide favourable outcomes by total outcomes in the sample space.

probe.question: A die is rolled. P(getting a 5)?

misconceptions.root_belief: ratio compares parts, not part to whole
misconceptions.source_hint: research on odds versus probability confusion in school students

misconceptions.statement: Probability of drawing a heart from a deck is 13/39.
misconceptions.why: Students subtract the favourable count from the total in the denominator.
misconceptions.fix: The denominator is all 52 cards, so P = 13/52 = 1/4.

probe.question: A card is drawn from 52 cards. P(heart)?

misconceptions.root_belief: only counted items belong in the total

misconceptions.statement: A probability can be greater than 1, like 5/4.
misconceptions.why: Students do not link probability with part of the whole.
misconceptions.fix: Favourable outcomes cannot exceed total outcomes, so probability is at most 1.

probe.question: Can P(E) = 5/4?

misconceptions.root_belief: numbers can grow without a limit

misconceptions.statement: A probability of 1/2 is bigger than 3/4 because 2 is bigger than 4's... denominators decide.
misconceptions.why: Students compare fractions by the denominator or numerator alone.
misconceptions.fix: 3/4 = 0.75 is greater than 1/2 = 0.5, so the event with 3/4 is more likely.

probe.question: Which is more likely: probability 1/3 or 1/2?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on whole-number bias in comparing fractions

misconceptions.statement: An event with probability 0 is just very unlikely but can still happen.
misconceptions.why: Students treat 0 as 'rare' rather than 'impossible'.
misconceptions.fix: Probability 0 means the event cannot happen in this experiment; 1 means it must happen.

probe.question: What is the probability of rolling a 7 on a die, and can it happen?
probe.wrong_answer: 0, but it can still happen once

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Probability of 1/2 means the event is impossible or sure, as nothing is in between.
misconceptions.why: Students think only 'will' or 'won't' answers exist.
misconceptions.fix: Values between 0 and 1 describe events that may or may not happen; larger means more likely.

probe.question: Is an event with P=1/2 certain, impossible or neither?
probe.wrong_answer: It must be one of the two

misconceptions.root_belief: outcomes are either certain or impossible
misconceptions.source_hint: Konold outcome approach: probability interpreted as yes/no prediction

misconceptions.statement: The probabilities of all outcomes of an experiment add up to the number of outcomes.
misconceptions.why: Students think each probability is 1 or confuse sums with counts.
misconceptions.fix: All elementary event probabilities add up to exactly 1.

probe.question: For a die, what do the six probabilities add up to?

misconceptions.root_belief: adding parts gives the count not the whole

misconceptions.statement: An event can contain only one outcome.
misconceptions.why: Students identify 'event' with the single result of one throw.
misconceptions.fix: An event can be one outcome or many, like 'even number' which has 2, 4 and 6.

probe.question: How many outcomes are in the event 'a prime number on a die'?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: If P(E) = 0.3 then P(not E) = 0.3 too, since they are opposite.
misconceptions.why: Students think opposite events share equal chance.

probe.question: P(win)=0.3. Find P(not win).

misconceptions.root_belief: two options means fifty-fifty

misconceptions.statement: P(E) + P(not E) = 100 or any fixed counting number such as 2.
misconceptions.why: Students mix probability sums with percentages or counts.
misconceptions.fix: P(E) + P(not E) = 1 always.

probe.question: If P(E)=2/5, find P(not E).

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The complement of 'getting a 6' on a die is 'getting a 1'.
misconceptions.why: Students take an opposite value, not everything else.
misconceptions.fix: The complement is all outcomes except 6: 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, so P = 5/6.

probe.question: Find P(not getting 6) on a die.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on complement and negation errors in probability language
